Nṛsiṁha-tāpinī Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Among the minor उपनिषद्स् those of the Tāpinī group have an important place. They mostly deal with the details connected with the upāsanās (meditations) of the particular deity whose name they bear.
The Nṛsiṁha-tāpinī Upaniṣad—like the other similar Upaniṣads—is also in two parts: the Pūrva and the Uttara. The former has a bhāṣya (commentary) ascribed to शङ्कर (A.
-820) whereas the latter has one called Dīpikā by the sage विद्यारण्य (A.

-1386). Upaniṣad Brahmayogin has also commented on them.
The Pūrva has been divided into five sections, each being called an ‘Upaniṣad,’ and having a total of 77 mantras. They are mostly in prose, interspersed occasionally with Ṛgvedic mantras.
It is assigned to the Atharvaveda and begins with the well-known śāntimantra (peace-chant), ‘bhadraṁ karṇebhiḥ’.
Before च्रेअतिओन् there were only vast causal waters. प्रजापति, the creator, was manifested out of the navel-lotus of the Supreme Lord नारायण. He desired to create this world and did तपस् (austerity). He then saw—or realised or obtained—the famous Nārasiṁhamantra, the king or the crown-jewel of all mantras, in the anuṣṭubh metre. He then created the whole world out of the power of that मन्त्र.
[Neither the Upaniṣad nor the commentators give the actual Nārasiṁha-mantra in the anuṣṭubh metre which is sung as a sāma. The actual मन्त्र as found in some मन्त्र-śāstra works is:
ugraṁ vīram mahāviṣṇuṁ
jvalantaṁ sarvatomukham ।
nṛsiṁham bhīṣaṇam bhadram
mṛtyumṛtyuṁ namāmyaham ॥
(Prapañcasārasārasaṅgraha 23)
It means: ‘I bow down to Nṛsiṁha (the Man-lion इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु) who is terrible, valorous, blazing (like the fire or the sun), all-pervading, awful, death of even the god of death, and yet, the ever-auspicious Mahāviṣṇu!’
Though there are other mantras of Nṛsiṁha in other metres like the गायत्री, it is this मन्त्र in the anuṣṭubh metre that is meant in this Upaniṣad. In this metre there are four pādas or quarters and 32 akṣaras or syllables. This factor should be kept in मिन्द् while studying the concepts given later, in this work.]
The Upaniṣad then compares or considers the entire earth, the demigods in the अन्तरिक्ष (sky or upper regions), the dyuloka (heavenly regions including the gods like वसुस्, Rudras and Ādityas) and ब्रह्मन्, the pure, as the four pādas or quarters of the Anuṣṭubh (the Nārasiṁha-mantra).
This analogy is then extended to the four वेदस् also.
Then comes a eulogy of the greatness of the repetition of this मन्त्र by describing the wonderful results one gets.
The identification of various beings and things in this universe—like fire, gods, vital-airs, sun, मोओन्, the trinity and so on—with the four pādas of the मन्त्र is further continued.
The जप (repetition) of this मन्त्र, it is then stated, will result in the vision of that deity.
Thus ends the first section.
The second section describes how the gods in हेअवेन्, being afraid of transmigratory existence, approached प्रजापति who taught them this मन्त्र. By that, they conquered sin and death.
The description of meditation on the four parts of प्रणव (a, u, m and half-syllable at the end) as identified with the four वेदस् and some other objects like the गार्हपत्य fire or gods like विष्णु and रुद्र comes next.
How to use the मन्त्र for nyāsas (See NYĀSA for details.) along with the syllable Om is described thereafter.
Then follows a detailed exposition of each of the words contained in the मन्त्र, like ugra, vīra, विष्णु and so on.
Since man (nṛ) is the best of higher living beings and the lion (siṁha) the best of the lower kind, he assumed the form of Nṛsiṁha, to show that he is the very best of च्रेअतिओन् in all its aspects.
The third section begins with the question of the देवस् or gods (in हेअवेन्) to प्रजापति regarding the शक्ति (power) and the बीज (seed) of the Nārasiṁha-mantra. प्रजापति replies that māyā-power of the Lord is the शक्ति and आकाश (sky or ether) is the बीज. It is because of the māyā-power that प्रजापति can create and it is from आकाश (the first product) that everything else proceeds.
The fourth section deals with the aṅgamantras (mantras subsidiary to the main one) which are: Om; the सावित्री of Yajurveda (same as the first part of Māhā-नारायण Upaniṣad 15.2); the लक्ष्मी-मन्त्र of Yajurveda (Oṁ bhūrlakṣmī and so on).
Then the famous Nṛsiṁhagāyatrī मन्त्र is narrated. It is:
oṁ nṛsiṁhāya vidmahe
vajranakhāya dhīmahi
tannaḥ siṁhaḥ pracodayāt ॥
The fifth section describes the famous सुदर्शनचक्र (discus) of Lord नरसिṁह (an aspect of Mahāviṣṇu). It may have six spokes or eight or twelve or sixteen or even thirty two with corresponding teeth. The esoteric meditations connected with them are also described.
This is then followed by a fairly long phalaśruti, the statement of the results one gets by repeating the Nārasiṁha-mantra. As a sample a few such results may be stated:
One who repeats this मन्त्र becomes purified, as if by the five elements. He crosses over all sins and conquers even death. He can prevent the five elements from exercising their power by over-powering them. He can attract to himself other beings like the demigods (yakṣas, नागस् and the ग्रहस् or planetary deities) as also the gods. He ultimately attains the highest abode of Lord विष्णु.
The Uttaratāpinī of the same Upaniṣad has nine khaṇḍas or sections and 84 mantras, all in prose, except for occasional quotations from the वेदस्.
This work, almost entirely, teaches Advaita Vedānta. The topics can be summarised very briefly as follows:
Identity of आत्मन् and ब्रह्मन्; the four states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, the fourth being the आत्मन्; meditation on the आत्मन् with the help of Oṁ or प्रणव; gods conquering the demons with the help of the Nṛsiṁhamantra; च्रेअतिओन् of the world by ब्रह्मन् with the māyā-power and entering into it; the gods deciding to acquire the knowledge (or experience) of the Advayātman, the one आत्मन् without a second; प्रजापति teaching it to them.
Thus ends this Upaniṣad.
